# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical reading of the Varden and Halden 24-month follow-up

This is the most informative of the five documents. It answers the open questions I flagged after the nine-month report:

- whether the gain lasts,
- whether timesheets miss work,
- whether the meetings association survives a registered test,
- what the counter arm costs,
- how waiting times compare with control.

It also corrects both the Varga and Holm comment and the meta-analysis fairly.

It still has weak points. The summary compares two different hours measures. The mediation result is stronger in wording than in design. The log-based hours measure sits awkwardly with the meetings mechanism. And the control group was partly contaminated, which complicates the "decay" reading.

## Arithmetic check

| Figure | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Output per timesheet hour | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Output per log hour | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden continuers | 0.968 / 0.866 = 1.118 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100 ✓ |

## What it settles

1. **The gain persists, but smaller.** With record-based output, randomisation and system-log hours, the per-hour gain is +8.5% (95% CI +3.4 to +13.8) at two years. That directly refutes the claim that the gain is "entirely an artifact."
2. **The meta-analysis's no-decay claim is undercut.** All four long-follow-up studies in that review were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That is exactly the weakness I raised about its duration subgroup.
3. **Coverage-bound work.** The county ended the counter arm. Waiting times were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices. Restoring service would have needed about 12% more staff, which matches the 11.4% per-employee output loss: 1/0.886 means about 13% more staff to hold output.
4. **Unrecorded work is small.** Logs show hours fell 11%, against 12% on timesheets.
5. **Meeting time was balanced at baseline.** Treated offices averaged 7.4 hours and control 7.2. This answers my earlier worry that only month-six data existed.

## Problems

### 1. The summary mixes two hours measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% is per timesheet hour and the 8.5% is per log hour. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%, a fall of about a fifth, not a third.

The body and Section 5 get this right. The summary, which is what people will quote, overstates the decline.

### 2. The decline is not statistically established

- The intervals overlap heavily: +6.9 to +18.4 at nine months and +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months.
- "Consistent with some fading" is fair wording.
- "Declined by about a quarter" in Section 5 states a point-estimate change as if it were a finding.

There are still only 7 offices per arm. The report doesn't say whether it corrected for having so few clusters, which I raised for the nine-month report. Its confidence intervals may therefore be too narrow, and that applies to "excludes zero by a clear margin" as well.

### 3. Control-group contamination makes the fade partly a control-group effect

Two control offices cut their meetings in month 15 and gained 4.1% in output per hour. Spread across 7 control offices, that is roughly a 1.2-point improvement in the control average, unweighted, over part of the period.

Because the estimate compares treated offices with control, part of the apparent fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may be the control group improving, not the treatment fading. The report treats the meeting audit as a promising side observation but never connects it to the decay estimate.

Two analyses would help:

- re-estimate the effect excluding those two offices, and
- report treated offices against their own baseline.

The meeting figures also look odd. If those two offices were at 5.0 hours, the control average of 7.0 implies the other five averaged about 7.8 hours. That is up from about 7.2 at baseline. Either meetings rose in those five offices, or the audit's effect had faded by month 24. The report should say which.

### 4. The log-based hours measure seems to conflict with the meetings mechanism

The new hours measure is "active log-in time on the case-management system." That most likely captures time spent on cases and leaves out meetings. If so, a rough check suggests a problem.

| | Control | Treated |
|---|---|---|
| Timesheet hours | ~37.9 | ~33.4 |
| Meetings | 7.0 | 3.9 |
| Non-meeting time | ~30.9 | ~29.5 |

Non-meeting time fell only about 5%, yet log hours fell 11%.

The check assumes a control baseline near 37.9 hours, so it is approximate. Still, if logs measure case work, three things follow:

- the 11% figure is hard to square with the meeting data;
- the logs are not a "stricter" version of the timesheet measure but a different quantity;
- cutting meetings should mainly raise output per *total* hour, not per *case-work* hour, unless the benefit is fewer interruptions.

Since the registered outcome is output per log-measured hour, the report needs to state exactly what the logs count. That bears on both the 8.5% figure and the mediation result.

### 5. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result

Registering the analysis before the 24-month outcomes was a real improvement. Four limitations remain.

- **Same offices.** The hypothesis came from these same 7 treated offices, and the analysis was registered at month 11, after 11 months of their data had been seen. It is a pre-specified test on the units that generated the hypothesis, not an independent replication. Varga and Holm's specific objection, a story fitted after the fact to a small group, is weakened but not answered.
- **Sample size.** A "larger sample of office-months" adds repeated measurements from the same offices, so there are still only 14 independent units. An interval as narrow as 28–66% seems tight for 7 treated offices unless the analysis properly accounts for clustering.
- **Measurement error.** Meetings come from calendars and are measured precisely. Fatigue comes from a self-reported scale, which is noisier. Measurement error pushes a mediator's estimated share down, so fatigue's 18% is likely underestimated. Some of the 35% "unexplained" may belong to it. The comparison is tilted toward meetings.
- **Confounding.** Neither mediator was randomised, which the limitations acknowledge. Managers who cut meetings may also have changed other things.

A fairer summary would be: "a pre-specified analysis supports meetings as the larger measured pathway."

### 6. Gaps still open from the nine-month report

- **Backlog and case age.** These are still not reported, even though the nine-month limitations named backlogs building up beyond statutory deadlines as a risk.
- **Cost per case including overtime.** Still not reported.
- **Quality and resignations.** Still given as levels without intervals: overturn rates of 3.2% against 3.0%, and resignations of 4.1% against 7.9%.
- **The 9% cost figure.** The counter-arm cost of +9% per contact against +12% staff isn't explained. It may net out savings from lower sickness or turnover, but the report should say.

### 7. The Halden subset

The authors' own caveat is fair and should be taken at its word: these organisations survived twice and are self-selected. Selection actually happened three times: completing the pilot, submitting records, and agreeing to follow-up (14 of 23). Two further points:

- The baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to Varga and Holm's figure for all 27 time-tracking organisations. Was each continuing organisation measured against its own baseline? If not, the 11.8% is not a valid figure for this subset.
- One reverter is a marketing agency that cited client deadlines. That is not coverage-bound work in the meta-analysis's sense. It suggests the discretionary/coverage-bound split misses a third category: work with external, client-set deadlines.

### 8. Disclosure

R. Okafor co-led the Halden pilot, whose working paper misdescribed when organisations withdrew. The section on earlier claims accepts Varga and Holm's measurement points but does not mention the attrition misreport. A brief acknowledgement would strengthen the report's credibility.

## Where things now stand

| Question | Best current answer | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in queue-based work at 2 years | ~8–10% (controlled, records, logs) | Moderate; one trial, 7 offices per arm |
| Output per worker, queue-based work | about −3% (CI includes 0) | Moderate |
| Does the gain fade? | Possibly somewhat; partly confounded by control contamination | Low |
| Coverage-bound work | Output and service fall; ~12% more staff, ~9% higher cost per contact | High |
| Mechanism | Fewer meetings is the larger *measured* pathway; fatigue plausibly underestimated | Low–moderate |
| Can the gain be had without cutting hours? | Untested; two contaminated control offices hint at partial yes | Very low |

The most useful next study would add the arm this trial lacked: offices that cut meetings and reorganise work while keeping full hours. That would show whether the shorter week is itself the source of the gain or mainly the occasion that prompts the reorganisation that produces it. It is the one question no document in this set can answer.
